topic: Landing gear, wheels, brakes and tyres

notes.front: What is conventional landing gear?
notes.back: Tail wheel-type gear: the main gear sit forward of the centre of gravity and a third wheel assembly supports the tail.
notes.explanation: It is called conventional because many early aircraft used this arrangement.
notes.example: Like a DC-3 or a Pitts Special sitting nose-high on the ramp with its tail resting on a small wheel.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 13, Aircraft Landing Gear Systems, “Tail Wheel-Type Landing Gear”, p. 13-2
notes.evidence: Tail wheel-type landing gear is also known as conventional gear because many early aircraft use this type of arrangement. The main gear are located forward of the center of gravity, causing the tail to require support from a third wheel assembly.

notes.front: What is tandem landing gear?
notes.back: Gear whose main gear and tail gear are lined up along the aircraft’s longitudinal axis.
notes.explanation: Sailplanes commonly use it, many with only one real gear forward on the fuselage and a skid under the tail.
notes.example: Like the two wheels of a bicycle, one behind the other; the B-52 bomber is a real example.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 13, Aircraft Landing Gear Systems, “Tandem Landing Gear”, p. 13-2
notes.evidence: As the name implies, this type of landing gear has the main gear and tail gear aligned on the longitudinal axis of the aircraft. Sailplanes commonly use tandem gear, although many only have one actual gear forward on the fuselage with a skid under the tail.

notes.front: What is tricycle landing gear?
notes.back: The most common arrangement: main gear plus a nose gear.
notes.explanation: The handbook notes it is used on both large and small aircraft, for the benefits it brings.
notes.example: Like a Cessna 172 or a Learjet, each sitting level on a nose wheel and two main gear.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 13, Aircraft Landing Gear Systems, “Tricycle-Type Landing Gear”, p. 13-3
notes.evidence: The most commonly used landing gear arrangement is the tricycle-type landing gear. It is comprised of main gear and nose gear. [Figure 13-6] Tricycle-type landing gear is used on large and small aircraft with the following benefits:

notes.front: What is spring steel landing gear?
notes.back: Flexible spring steel (or aluminium or composite) struts that take the landing impact and return it to the airframe at a harmless rate.
notes.explanation: The gear flexes first, and the load is passed on as it springs back to its original position.
notes.example: Like a diving board that bends under a jumper and springs back, as on thousands of single-engine Cessnas.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 13, Aircraft Landing Gear Systems, “Leaf-Type Spring Gear”, p. 13-6
notes.evidence: Many aircraft utilize flexible spring steel, aluminum, or composite struts that receive the impact of landing and return it to the airframe to dissipate at a rate that is not harmful. The gear flexes initially and forces are transferred as it returns to its original position.

notes.front: What is rigid landing gear?
notes.back: Rigid, welded steel struts, used on many early aircraft before curved spring steel struts, that pass landing shock straight to the airframe.
notes.explanation: Only the pneumatic tyres help soften the impact loads.
notes.example: Like a bicycle with no suspension, where only the tyres soak up the bumps; helicopter skids are a modern case.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 13, Aircraft Landing Gear Systems, “Rigid”, p. 13-7
notes.evidence: Before the development of curved spring steel landing struts, many early aircraft were designed with rigid, welded steel landing gear struts. Shock load transfer to the airframe is direct with this design. Use of pneumatic tires aids in softening the impact loads.

notes.front: What is a shock strut?
notes.back: A self-contained hydraulic unit that supports the aircraft on the ground and protects the structure on landing by turning impact energy into heat.
notes.explanation: This conversion to heat is true shock absorption, the most common way of dissipating landing shock in aviation, on aircraft of all sizes.
notes.example: Like a car’s shock absorber, but it also carries the aircraft’s weight on a cushion of compressed air or nitrogen.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 13, Aircraft Landing Gear Systems, “Shock Struts”, p. 13-7
notes.evidence: True shock absorption occurs when the shock energy of landing impact is converted into heat energy, as in a shock strut landing gear. This is the most common method of landing shock dissipation in aviation. It is used on aircraft of all sizes.

notes.front: What is a metering pin?
notes.back: A tapered pin in a shock strut’s orifice that automatically controls how fast fluid flows during compression.
notes.explanation: Where the narrow part of the pin sits in the orifice more fluid passes; as the diameter in the orifice grows, less passes.
notes.example: Like a tapered needle slowly pushed into a funnel’s spout, narrowing the gap the further it goes.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 13, Aircraft Landing Gear Systems, “Shock Struts”, p. 13-8
notes.evidence: It is automatically controlled by the taper of the metering pin in the orifice. When a narrow portion of the pin is in the orifice, more fluid can pass to the upper chamber. As the diameter of the portion of the metering pin in the orifice increases, less fluid passes.

notes.front: What is a torque link?
notes.back: One of a pair of hinged links (torque arms) joining a shock strut’s fixed upper cylinder to its piston so the piston cannot rotate.
notes.explanation: Holding the piston against rotation is what keeps the piston and wheels aligned.
notes.example: Like the folding scissor arms of a trellis gate, but here they stop a strut piston from twisting.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 13, Aircraft Landing Gear Systems, “Shock Struts”, p. 13-9
notes.evidence: To keep the piston and wheels aligned, most shock struts are equipped with torque links or torque arms. One end of the links is attached to the fixed upper cylinder. The other end is attached to the lower cylinder (piston), so it cannot rotate.

notes.front: What is a landing gear trunnion?
notes.back: A fixed structural extension of the upper strut cylinder with bearing surfaces on which the whole gear assembly moves.
notes.explanation: It is attached to structure so the gear can pivot from vertical, for landing and taxi, to its stowed position in flight.
notes.example: Like the hinge pins a door swings on, but carrying a landing gear leg.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 13, Aircraft Landing Gear Systems, “Support”, p. 13-17
notes.evidence: The trunnion is a fixed structural extension of the upper strut cylinder with bearing surfaces that allow the entire gear assembly to move. It is attached to aircraft structure in such a way that the gear can pivot from the vertical position required for landing and taxi to the stowed position used during flight.

notes.front: What is a squat switch?
notes.back: A landing gear safety switch that opens and closes as the main gear strut extends or compresses.
notes.explanation: It is wired into many system circuits; one prevents the gear from being retracted while the aircraft is on the ground.
notes.example: Like a pressure mat at a shop door, but telling aircraft systems whether weight is on the wheels.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 13, Aircraft Landing Gear Systems, “Safety Switch”, p. 13-22
notes.evidence: This is a switch positioned to open and close depending on the extension or compression of the main landing gear strut. [Figure 13-39] The squat switch is wired into any number of system operating circuits. One circuit prevents the gear from being retracted while the aircraft is on the ground.

notes.front: What is a landing gear ground lock?
notes.back: An external device placed in the retraction mechanism to stop it moving, so the gear stays down and locked on the ground.
notes.explanation: It is extra insurance on top of the gear’s own locks.
notes.example: Like a steering-wheel lock on a parked car, but it pins the gear so it cannot fold.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 13, Aircraft Landing Gear Systems, “Ground Locks”, p. 13-22
notes.evidence: Ground locks are commonly used on aircraft landing gear as extra insurance that the landing gear will remain down and locked while the aircraft is on the ground. They are external devices that are placed in the retraction mechanism to prevent its movement.

notes.front: What is a shimmy damper?
notes.back: A unit that controls nose wheel shimmy, a rapid oscillation at certain speeds, through hydraulic damping.
notes.explanation: Torque links alone are not enough to stop most nose gear from shimmying.
notes.example: Like the steering damper on a motorbike that stops a speed wobble, but fitted to a nose gear.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 13, Aircraft Landing Gear Systems, “Shimmy Dampers”, p. 13-30
notes.evidence: are not sufficient to prevent most nose gear from the tendency to oscillate rapidly, or shimmy, at certain speeds. This vibration must be controlled through the use of a shimmy damper. A shimmy damper controls nose wheel shimmy through hydraulic damping.

notes.front: What is a split wheel?
notes.back: A two-piece wheel, cast or forged from aluminium or magnesium alloy, whose halves bolt together with an O-ring groove at the mating surface.
notes.explanation: The O-ring seals the rim, which is needed because most modern aircraft use tubeless tyres.
notes.example: Like two shallow bowls bolted rim to rim, with the tyre fitted over the joint.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 13, Aircraft Landing Gear Systems, “Wheel Construction”, p. 13-34
notes.evidence: The typical modern two-piece aircraft wheel is cast or forged from aluminum or magnesium alloy. The halves are bolted together and contain a groove at the mating surface for an o-ring, which seals the rim since most modern aircraft utilize tubeless tires.

notes.front: What is a fusible plug in an aircraft wheel?
notes.back: A threaded thermal plug whose core melts at a lower temperature than the rest of the plug, letting air out of the tyre.
notes.explanation: It releases the air should tyre temperature rise to a dangerous level.
notes.example: Like the heat-sensitive bulb in a fire sprinkler, but it opens to let tyre air out instead of water in.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 13, Aircraft Landing Gear Systems, “Fusible Plug Inspection”, p. 13-41
notes.evidence: Fusible plugs or thermal plugs must be inspected visually. These threaded plugs have a core that melts at a lower temperature than the outer part of the plug. This is to release air from the tire should the temperature rise to a dangerous level.

notes.front: What is brinelling of a bearing?
notes.back: Indentations in the bearing cup raceways, caused by excessive impact.
notes.explanation: Any static overload or severe impact can cause true brinelling, which leads to vibration and premature bearing failure.
notes.example: Like dents hammered into a railway track, so every roller bumps as it passes.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 13, Aircraft Landing Gear Systems, “Wheel Bearing Inspection”, p. 13-39
notes.evidence: Brinelling is caused by excessive impact. It appears as indentations in the bearing cup raceways. Any static overload or severe impact can cause true brinelling, which leads to vibration and premature bearing failure.

notes.front: What is a single disc brake?
notes.back: One disc keyed or bolted to each wheel, gripped on both sides by a non-rotating caliper bolted to the axle flange.
notes.explanation: It is how small, light aircraft typically get effective braking.
notes.example: Like a bicycle disc brake, where a fixed caliper squeezes a disc that turns with the wheel.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 13, Aircraft Landing Gear Systems, “Types & Construction of Aircraft Brakes”, p. 13-42
notes.evidence: Small, light aircraft typically achieve effective braking using a single disc keyed or bolted to each wheel. As the wheel turns, so does the disc. Braking is accomplished by applying friction to both sides of the disc from a non-rotating caliper bolted to the landing gear axle flange.

notes.front: What is a multiple-disc brake?
notes.back: A heavy-duty brake with steel stators keyed to the bearing carrier alternating with copper- or bronze-plated rotors keyed to the wheel.
notes.explanation: Large, heavy aircraft need this type, which is built for power brake control valves or power boost master cylinders.
notes.example: Like a stack of alternating coins and washers squeezed together, some turning and some held still.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 13, Aircraft Landing Gear Systems, “Multiple-Disc Brakes”, p. 13-46
notes.evidence: Large, heavy aircraft require the use of multiple-disc brakes. Multiple-disc brakes are heavy duty brakes designed for use with power brake control valves or power boost master cylinders, which is discussed later in this chapter.

notes.front: What is a segmented rotor brake?
notes.back: A multiple-disc brake whose rotors are slotted or built in sections, rubbing against stationary high-friction linings.
notes.explanation: The spaces between the rotor sections help dissipate heat and give the brake its name.
notes.example: Like a stack of discs with gaps cut into them, where the gaps shed braking heat.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 13, Aircraft Landing Gear Systems, “Segmented Rotor-Disc Brakes”, p. 13-46
notes.evidence: Braking is accomplished by means of several sets of stationary, high friction type brake linings that make contact with rotating segments. The rotors are constructed with slots or in sections with space between them, which helps dissipate heat and give the brake its name.

notes.front: What is a carbon brake?
notes.back: The latest multiple-disc brake, with rotors built from carbon fibre materials; found on high-performance and air carrier aircraft.
notes.explanation: It is the newest step in the evolution of the multiple-disc brake rather than a separate family.
notes.example: Like the carbon discs of a racing car, but stacked as rotors in a multiple-disc aircraft brake.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 13, Aircraft Landing Gear Systems, “Carbon Brakes”, p. 13-49
notes.evidence: The latest iteration of the multiple-disc brake is the carbon-disc brake. It is currently found on high performance and air carrier aircraft. Carbon brakes are so named because carbon fiber materials are used to construct the brake rotors.

notes.front: What is an expander tube brake?
notes.back: An older brake whose fluid-filled neoprene tube expands outward, pressing brake blocks against the wheel drum.
notes.explanation: Raising the hydraulic pressure in the tube raises the friction against the drum.
notes.example: Like a bicycle inner tube pumped up inside a drum, but pumped with hydraulic fluid.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 13, Aircraft Landing Gear Systems, “Expander Tube Brakes”, p. 13-49
notes.evidence: Hydraulic fluid under pressure is directed through this fitting into the inside of the tube when the brakes are applied. The tube expands outward, and the brake blocks make contact with the wheel drum causing friction that slows the wheel. As hydraulic pressure is increased, greater friction develops.

notes.front: What is a brake master cylinder?
notes.back: A pedal-operated cylinder that develops the hydraulic pressure for the brakes in an independent brake system.
notes.explanation: An independent system has no connection to the aircraft hydraulic system, so it needs its own source of pressure.
notes.example: Like the master cylinder behind a car’s brake pedal, but light aircraft usually have one per rudder pedal.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 13, Aircraft Landing Gear Systems, “Independent Master Cylinders”, p. 13-51
notes.evidence: An independent brake system is not connected in any way to the aircraft hydraulic system. Master cylinders are used to develop the necessary hydraulic pressure to operate the brakes. This is similar to the brake system of an automobile.

notes.front: What is a master cylinder’s compensating port?
notes.back: A port in most master cylinders that lets brake fluid expand safely into the reservoir when the brakes are not applied.
notes.explanation: Without it, trapped fluid could make a brake drag against its rotor, or cause leaks.
notes.example: Like the overflow pipe of a hot-water tank, giving warmed fluid somewhere to go.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 13, Aircraft Landing Gear Systems, “Independent Master Cylinders”, p. 13-52
notes.evidence: fluid can cause a brake to drag against the rotor(s). Leaks may also result. When the brakes are not applied, fluid must be allowed to expand safely without causing these issues. A compensating port is included in most master cylinders to facilitate this.

notes.front: What is a boosted brake system?
notes.back: A brake system that adds aircraft hydraulic system pressure to the pilot’s foot force, but only during heavy braking.
notes.explanation: The result is more brake pressure than the pilot’s foot alone could give.
notes.example: Like power steering that only helps when you turn the wheel hard.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 13, Aircraft Landing Gear Systems, “Boosted Brakes”, p. 13-54
notes.evidence: Boosted brake actuating systems augment the force developed by the pilot with hydraulic system pressure when needed. The boost is only during heavy braking. It results in greater pressure applied to the brakes than the pilot alone can provide.

notes.front: What is a power brake system?
notes.back: A brake system that uses the aircraft hydraulic system as its source of power to apply the brakes.
notes.explanation: A master cylinder cannot produce the fluid volume and pressure these brakes need; the pilot still presses the pedal tops.
notes.example: Like a lorry’s brakes, where the pedal only opens a valve and the vehicle’s own system does the pushing.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 13, Aircraft Landing Gear Systems, “Power Brakes”, p. 13-55
notes.evidence: Power brake actuating systems use the aircraft hydraulic system as the source of power to apply the brakes. The pilot presses on the top of the rudder pedal for braking as with the other actuating systems. The volume and pressure of hydraulic fluid required cannot be produced by a master cylinder.

notes.front: What does an anti-skid system do?
notes.back: It detects a wheel skid, or an imminent one, and briefly relieves that wheel’s brake pressure to the hydraulic return line.
notes.explanation: Relieving the pressure lets the wheel rotate and avoid the skid.
notes.example: Like a car’s anti-lock brakes, but acting wheel by wheel on a multi-wheel main gear.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 13, Aircraft Landing Gear Systems, “System Operation”, p. 13-60
notes.evidence: The anti-skid system not only detects wheel skid, it also detects when wheel skid is imminent. It automatically relieves pressure to the brake pistons of the wheel in question by momentarily connecting the pressurized brake fluid area to the hydraulic system return line. This allows the wheel to rotate and avoid a skid.

notes.front: What is a wheel speed sensor?
notes.back: The anti-skid sensor fitted to each wheel that has a brake, reporting that wheel’s speed.
notes.explanation: A single control box typically compares the signals for all the brakes on the aircraft.
notes.example: Like the wheel sensor behind a car’s anti-lock brakes, but an airliner has one on every braked wheel.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 13, Aircraft Landing Gear Systems, “System Operation”, p. 13-60
notes.evidence: Wheel speed sensors are located on each wheel equipped with a brake assembly. Each brake also has its own anti-skid control valve. Typically, a single control box contains the anti-skid comparative circuitry for all of the brakes on the aircraft.

notes.front: What is an anti-skid control valve?
notes.back: A fast-acting, electrically controlled hydraulic valve, one per brake assembly, that adjusts brake pressure on the control unit’s input.
notes.explanation: Because each brake has its own valve, pressure can be changed at one brake without the others.
notes.example: Like a tap turned by a small electric motor on a computer’s command.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 13, Aircraft Landing Gear Systems, “Anti-Skid Control Valves”, p. 13-63
notes.evidence: Anti-skid control valves are fast-acting, electrically controlled hydraulic valves that respond to the input from the anti-skid control unit. There is one control valve for each brake assembly.

notes.front: What is an autobrake system?
notes.back: A system that brakes the aircraft through its own auto brake control valve, bypassing the normal brake control or metering valves.
notes.explanation: Besides giving redundancy, it relies on the anti-skid system to reduce pressure if a skid is impending.
notes.example: Like cruise control in reverse: the pilot sets it, and the aircraft slows itself.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 13, Aircraft Landing Gear Systems, “Auto Brakes”, p. 13-64
notes.evidence: Aircraft equipped with auto brakes typically bypass the brake control valves or brake metering valves and use a separate auto brake control valve to provide this function. In addition to the redundancy provided, auto brakes rely on the anti-skid system to adjust pressure to the brakes if required due to an impending skid.

notes.front: What is a brake debooster?
notes.back: A cylinder fitted downstream of the control valve and anti-skid valve that lowers the pressure reaching the brake.
notes.explanation: Some brakes worked by the aircraft hydraulic system are not designed for full system pressure.
notes.example: Like a pressure-reducing valve on a mains water supply, but built from one piston with two ends of different sizes.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 13, Aircraft Landing Gear Systems, “Brake Deboosters”, p. 13-59
notes.evidence: Some aircraft brake assemblies that operate on aircraft hydraulic system pressure are not designed for such high pressure. They provide effective braking through a power brake system but require less than maximum hydraulic system pressure. To supply the lower pressure, a brake debooster cylinder is installed downstream of the control valve and anti-skid valve.

notes.front: What is a tyre’s ply rating?
notes.back: A figure conveying the tyre’s relative strength, whatever number of plies it actually contains.
notes.explanation: A high ply rating means a strong tyre able to carry heavy loads.
notes.example: Like the load index on a car tyre: a strength rating, not a count of layers.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 13, Aircraft Landing Gear Systems, “Ply Rating”, p. 13-75
notes.evidence: However, a ply rating is used to convey the relative strength of an aircraft tire. A tire with a high ply rating is a tire with high strength able to carry heavy loads regardless of the actual number of plies used in its construction.

notes.front: What is the bead of an aircraft tyre?
notes.back: The part that anchors the tyre carcass and gives a firm, dimensioned mounting surface on the wheel rim.
notes.explanation: The handbook stresses it as an important part: the tyre’s whole seat on the rim depends on it.
notes.example: Like the stiff wire edge of a bicycle tyre that hooks onto the rim, but with up to three steel wire bundles a side.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 13, Aircraft Landing Gear Systems, “Bead”, p. 13-76
notes.evidence: The tire bead is an important part of an aircraft tire. It anchors the tire carcass and provides a dimensioned, firm mounting surface for the tire on the wheel rim.

notes.front: What is a chine tyre?
notes.back: A tyre whose sidewall is mounded into a built-in deflector (a chine) that throws runway water sideways.
notes.explanation: It keeps the water away from engine intakes, so it is used on nose wheels, usually of aircraft with fuselage-mounted engines.
notes.example: Like a mudguard moulded into the tyre itself, sending spray away from rear-mounted jet engines.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 13, Aircraft Landing Gear Systems, “Chine”, p. 13-78
notes.evidence: A chine is a special built-in deflector used on nose wheels of certain aircraft, usually those with fuselage mounted engines. The chine diverts runway water to the side and away from the intake of the engines.

notes.front: What is a sidewall vent on an aircraft tyre?
notes.back: A vent hole in the lower outer sidewall, usually marked with a green or white paint dot, releasing gas that seeps into the plies.
notes.explanation: The inner liner does not hold all the inflation gas, so some seeps into the carcass plies and needs a way out.
notes.example: Like the weep holes at the foot of a brick wall, but letting trapped gas out rather than water.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 13, Aircraft Landing Gear Systems, “Inflation”, p. 13-78
notes.evidence: The inner liner does not contain 100 percent of the inflation gas. Small amounts of nitrogen or air seep through the liner into the carcass plies. This seepage is released through vent holes in the lower outer sidewall of the tires. These are typically marked with a green or white dot of paint and must be kept unobstructed.

notes.front: What is hydroplaning?
notes.back: Loss of tyre contact with the runway because the tyre is running on water; steering and braking are lost too.
notes.explanation: In dynamic hydroplaning, water building up in front of the tyre gives it a surface to ride on.
notes.example: Like a car aquaplaning through standing water on a motorway.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 13, Aircraft Landing Gear Systems, “Hydroplaning”, p. 13-92
notes.evidence: Water building up in front of the tire provides a surface for the tire to run on and contact with the runway surface is lost. This is known as dynamic hydroplaning. Steering ability and braking action is also lost.

notes.front: The three basic landing gear arrangements are tail wheel-type, tandem and {{c1::tricycle-type}}.
notes.explanation: Tail wheel-type gear is the one also known as conventional gear.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 13, Aircraft Landing Gear Systems, “Landing Gear Arrangement”, p. 13-2
notes.evidence: Three basic arrangements of landing gear are used: tail wheel-type landing gear (also known as conventional gear), tandem landing gear, and tricycle-type landing gear.

notes.front: Besides the gear legs and wheels, name three things the handbook counts as parts of the landing gear system.
notes.back: Among others: shock absorbing equipment, brakes and retraction mechanisms.
notes.explanation: The list also includes controls, warning devices, cowling, fairings and the structural members that attach the gear.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 13, Aircraft Landing Gear Systems, “Landing Gear Types”, p. 13-1
notes.evidence: Regardless of the type of landing gear utilized, shock absorbing equipment, brakes, retraction mechanisms, controls, warning devices, cowling, fairings, and structural members necessary to attach the gear to the aircraft are considered parts of the landing gear system.

notes.front: What does “auxiliary landing gear” refer to?
notes.back: The nose gear, tail gear or outrigger-type gear.
notes.explanation: Main gear, by contrast, are the two or more large gear close to the centre of gravity.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 13, Aircraft Landing Gear Systems, “Landing Gear Types”, p. 13-1
notes.evidence: Note: References to auxiliary landing gear refer to the nose gear, tail gear, or outrigger-type gear on any particular aircraft. Main landing gear are the two or more large gear located close to the aircraft’s center of gravity.

notes.front: A sailplane has one wheel under the forward fuselage and a skid under its tail, all on the centreline. Which arrangement is this?
notes.back: B) Tandem landing gear
notes.choices:
A) Tricycle landing gear
B) Tandem landing gear
C) Conventional landing gear
D) Outrigger gear
notes.choicesExplained: A: tricycle gear needs main gear plus a nose gear. C: conventional gear has main gear forward of the centre of gravity with the tail on a wheel or skid, not one wheel on the centreline. D: outrigger gear is small support gear under the wings, as on the Harrier.
notes.explanation: Wheel and tail skid both sit on the longitudinal axis, the defining feature of tandem gear, which sailplanes commonly use.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 13, Aircraft Landing Gear Systems, “Tandem Landing Gear”, p. 13-2
notes.evidence: Sailplanes commonly use tandem gear, although many only have one actual gear forward on the fuselage with a skid under the tail.

notes.front: Give two reasons aircraft are still built with conventional landing gear today.
notes.back: Extra forward fuselage clearance for unpaved runways, and the weight saved by the light tail wheel assembly.
notes.explanation: The clearance comes from the nose-high angle of the fuselage that tail wheel gear produces.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 13, Aircraft Landing Gear Systems, “Tail Wheel-Type Landing Gear”, p. 13-2
notes.evidence: The increased clearance of the forward fuselage offered by tail wheel-type landing gear is also advantageous when operating in and out of non-paved runways. Today, aircraft are manufactured with conventional gear for this reason and for the weight savings accompanying the relatively light tail wheel assembly.

notes.front: The fuselage angle of an aircraft on conventional gear allows a {{c1::long propeller}}, which compensated for older, underpowered engines.
notes.explanation: Tail wheel gear holds the nose high, giving the propeller room.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 13, Aircraft Landing Gear Systems, “Tail Wheel-Type Landing Gear”, p. 13-2
notes.evidence: The resulting angle of the aircraft fuselage, when fitted with conventional gear, allows the use of a long propeller that compensates for older, underpowered engine

notes.front: On conventional gear, how is directional control kept before the rudder becomes effective?
notes.back: By differential braking; many designs also have a steerable tail wheel linked by cables to the rudder or rudder pedals.
notes.explanation: The rudder only takes over once the aircraft is moving fast enough.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 13, Aircraft Landing Gear Systems, “Tail Wheel-Type Landing Gear”, p. 13-2
notes.evidence: Directional control is maintained through differential braking until the speed of the aircraft enables control with the rudder. A steerable tail wheel, connected by cables to the rudder or rudder pedals, is also a common design.

notes.front: Hard-surface runways have made the tail {{c1::skid}} obsolete in favour of the tail wheel.
notes.explanation: A few early designs used a skid, which helped slow the aircraft on landing on soft fields.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 13, Aircraft Landing Gear Systems, “Tail Wheel-Type Landing Gear”, p. 13-2
notes.evidence: The proliferation of hard surface runways has rendered the tail skid obsolete in favor of the tail wheel.

notes.front: A mechanic walks round an aircraft whose two main wheels sit ahead of its centre of gravity and whose tail rests on a small steerable wheel. What gear is this?
notes.back: C) Conventional landing gear
notes.choices:
A) Tandem landing gear
B) Tricycle landing gear
C) Conventional landing gear
D) Rigid landing gear
notes.choicesExplained: A: tandem gear lines main and tail gear up on the longitudinal axis. B: tricycle gear has its centre of gravity ahead of the main gear and a nose wheel. D: rigid gear describes how the strut handles shock, not the wheel arrangement.
notes.explanation: Main gear forward of the centre of gravity, with a third wheel assembly carrying the tail, is tail wheel-type gear.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 13, Aircraft Landing Gear Systems, “Tail Wheel-Type Landing Gear”, p. 13-2
notes.evidence: The main gear are located forward of the center of gravity, causing the tail to require support from a third wheel assembly.

notes.front: What does putting all the gear under the fuselage, as with tandem gear, generally make possible?
notes.back: Very flexible wings.
notes.explanation: The Harrier shows the trade-off: tandem gear, plus small outrigger gear under the wings for support.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 13, Aircraft Landing Gear Systems, “Tandem Landing Gear”, p. 13-2
notes.evidence: The VTOL Harrier has tandem gear but uses small outrigger gear under the wings for support. Generally, placing the gear only under the fuselage facilitates the use of very flexible wings.

notes.front: Which benefit of tricycle gear allows higher landing speeds?
notes.back: The brakes can be applied more forcefully without the aircraft nosing over.
notes.explanation: Harder braking without nosing over is what makes the higher landing speeds usable.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 13, Aircraft Landing Gear Systems, “Tricycle-Type Landing Gear”, p. 13-3
notes.evidence: 1. Allows more forceful application of the brakes without nosing over when braking, which enables higher landing speeds.

notes.front: What does tricycle gear do for the view from the flight deck?
notes.back: It gives better visibility, especially during landing and ground manoeuvring.
notes.explanation: This is one of the three benefits the handbook lists for the arrangement.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 13, Aircraft Landing Gear Systems, “Tricycle-Type Landing Gear”, p. 13-3
notes.evidence: 2. Provides better visibility from the flight deck, especially during landing and ground maneuvering.

notes.front: Why does tricycle gear prevent ground-looping?
notes.back: The centre of gravity is forward of the main gear, so forces on it keep the aircraft moving forward rather than looping.
notes.explanation: The handbook contrasts this with tail wheel-type gear, which can loop.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 13, Aircraft Landing Gear Systems, “Tricycle-Type Landing Gear”, p. 13-3
notes.evidence: 3. Prevents ground-looping of the aircraft. Since the aircraft center of gravity is forward of the main gear, forces acting on the center of gravity tend to keep the aircraft moving forward rather than looping, such as with a tail wheel-type landing gear.

notes.front: A designer wants an aircraft that can brake hard on landing without nosing over and will not ground-loop. Which arrangement fits best?
notes.back: D) Tricycle landing gear
notes.choices:
A) Conventional landing gear
B) Tandem landing gear
C) Skid gear
D) Tricycle landing gear
notes.choicesExplained: A: tail wheel gear puts the centre of gravity behind the main gear, the set-up that loops. B: tandem gear is chosen for flexible wings, not braking. C: skids help slow an aircraft but offer no controlled wheel braking.
notes.explanation: Tricycle gear allows more forceful braking without nosing over, which also enables higher landing speeds.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 13, Aircraft Landing Gear Systems, “Tricycle-Type Landing Gear”, p. 13-3
notes.evidence: Tricycle-type landing gear is used on large and small aircraft with the following benefits: 1. Allows more forceful application of the brakes without nosing over when braking, which enables higher landing speeds.

notes.front: A nose wheel that cannot be controlled simply {{c1::casters}}, and the aircraft is steered with differential braking.
notes.explanation: Only a few aircraft are like this; nearly all have steerable nose gear.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 13, Aircraft Landing Gear Systems, “Tricycle-Type Landing Gear”, p. 13-3
notes.evidence: The nose gear of a few aircraft with tricycle-type landing gear is not controllable. It simply casters as steering is accomplished with differential braking during taxi. However, nearly all aircraft have steerable nose gear.

notes.front: Give two reasons for having several wheels on each main gear.
notes.back: They spread the aircraft’s weight over a larger area, and give a safety margin if one tyre fails.
notes.explanation: Heavy aircraft may use four or more wheel assemblies on each main gear.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 13, Aircraft Landing Gear Systems, “Tricycle-Type Landing Gear”, p. 13-4
notes.evidence: Multiple wheels spread the weight of the aircraft over a larger area. They also provide a safety margin should one tire fail. Heavy aircraft may use four or more wheel assemblies on each main gear.

notes.front: What is a bogie, and what decides how many wheels it has?
notes.back: The mounting for more than two wheels on one strut; wheel count depends on gross design weight and the landing surface.
notes.explanation: A bogie is simply how more than two wheels join one strut; design weight and landing surface set its size.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 13, Aircraft Landing Gear Systems, “Tricycle-Type Landing Gear”, p. 13-4
notes.evidence: When more than two wheels are attached to a landing gear strut, the attaching mechanism is known as a bogie. The number of wheels included in the bogie is a function of the gross design weight of the aircraft and the surface type on which the loaded aircraft is required to land.

notes.front: Why do slow aircraft keep fixed landing gear?
notes.back: On slow aircraft the extra weight of a retraction mechanism is not repaid by the drag it removes.
notes.explanation: Retracting gear removes parasite drag, but the mechanism adds weight to the aircraft.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 13, Aircraft Landing Gear Systems, “Fixed & Retractable Landing Gear”, p. 13-5
notes.evidence: Mechanisms to retract and stow the landing gear to eliminate parasite drag add weight to the aircraft. On slow aircraft, the penalty of this added weight is not overcome by the reduction of drag, so fixed gear is used.

notes.front: How can the parasite drag of fixed landing gear be reduced?
notes.back: By building the gear as aerodynamically as possible and adding fairings or wheel pants over the protruding parts.
notes.explanation: A small, smooth profile to the oncoming wind greatly reduces gear drag.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 13, Aircraft Landing Gear Systems, “Fixed & Retractable Landing Gear”, p. 13-5
notes.evidence: A great deal of the parasite drag caused by light aircraft landing gear can be reduced by building gear as aerodynamically as possible and by adding fairings or wheel pants to streamline the airflow past the protruding assemblies.

notes.front: The parasite drag of extended landing gear can be used by the pilot to {{c1::slow the aircraft}}.
notes.explanation: Retracted gear sits in wheel wells out of the slipstream, so extending it adds drag the pilot can use.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 13, Aircraft Landing Gear Systems, “Fixed & Retractable Landing Gear”, p. 13-6
notes.evidence: Note: The parasite drag caused by extended landing gear can be used by the pilot to slow the aircraft.

notes.front: The extension and retraction of most landing gear is usually done with {{c1::hydraulics}}.
notes.explanation: Retractable gear stows in fuselage or wing compartments in flight, and a hydraulic mechanism moves most of it.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 13, Aircraft Landing Gear Systems, “Fixed & Retractable Landing Gear”, p. 13-6
notes.evidence: The extension and retraction of most landing gear is usually accomplished with hydraulics.

notes.front: An owner of a slow, light bush aircraft asks whether converting it to retractable gear would help performance. What does the handbook’s reasoning suggest?
notes.back: A) Keep fixed gear: the weight penalty would outweigh the drag saved
notes.choices:
A) Keep fixed gear: the weight penalty would outweigh the drag saved
B) Retract the gear: any drag reduction improves performance
C) Fit tandem gear instead
D) Remove the fairings to save weight
notes.choicesExplained: B: retraction pays only once speed is high enough for gear drag to exceed the weight penalty. C: tandem gear is chosen for flexible wings, not drag. D: fairings and wheel pants reduce parasite drag on fixed gear.
notes.explanation: On slow aircraft the added weight of a retraction mechanism is not overcome by the drag reduction, so fixed gear stays the better choice.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 13, Aircraft Landing Gear Systems, “Fixed & Retractable Landing Gear”, p. 13-5
notes.evidence: On slow aircraft, the penalty of this added weight is not overcome by the reduction of drag, so fixed gear is used.

notes.front: What landing gear suits aircraft operating from frozen lakes and snowy areas?
notes.back: Skis.
notes.explanation: The type of gear depends on the aircraft design and its intended use.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 13, Aircraft Landing Gear Systems, “Landing Gear Types”, p. 13-1
notes.evidence: Aircraft that operate to and from frozen lakes and snowy areas may be equipped with landing gear that have skis.

notes.front: What landing gear do aircraft that operate from the surface of water have?
notes.back: Pontoon-type (float) gear.
notes.explanation: Floats or pontoons are one of the four basic gear types the handbook illustrates, alongside wheels, skids and skis.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 13, Aircraft Landing Gear Systems, “Landing Gear Types”, p. 13-1
notes.evidence: Aircraft that operate to and from the surface of water have pontoon-type landing gear.

notes.front: How does amphibious gear let an aircraft land on water or on a runway?
notes.back: It has pontoons for water landings, with extendable wheels for hard surfaces.
notes.explanation: Combining two types of gear on one aircraft is common.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 13, Aircraft Landing Gear Systems, “Landing Gear Types”, p. 13-1
notes.evidence: Amphibious aircraft are designed with gear that allow landings to be made on water or dry land. The gear features pontoons for water landing with extendable wheels for landings on hard surfaces.

notes.front: On aircraft that use both frozen surfaces and dry runways, the {{c1::skis}} are typically retractable so the wheels can be used.
notes.explanation: It is the same idea as amphibious gear, applied to snow and ice instead of water.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 13, Aircraft Landing Gear Systems, “Landing Gear Types”, p. 13-1
notes.evidence: A similar system is used to allow the use of skis and wheels on aircraft that operate on both slippery, frozen surfaces and dry runways. Typically, the skis are retractable to allow use of the wheels when needed.

notes.front: An operator flies charters from lakes in summer and must also use paved runways. Which gear lets one aircraft do both?
notes.back: D) Amphibious gear
notes.choices:
A) Plain floats
B) Wheel replacement skis
C) Tundra tyres
D) Amphibious gear
notes.choicesExplained: A: plain floats cannot land on a runway. B: skis are for snow and ice. C: larger tyres suit rough terrain, not water.
notes.explanation: Amphibious gear has pontoons for water plus extendable wheels for hard surfaces.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 13, Aircraft Landing Gear Systems, “Landing Gear Types”, p. 13-1
notes.evidence: Amphibious aircraft are designed with gear that allow landings to be made on water or dry land. The gear features pontoons for water landing with extendable wheels for landings on hard surfaces.

notes.front: AC 43.13-2C’s ski data for main and nose skis applies to which skis only?
notes.back: Wheel replacement skis.
notes.explanation: Tyre-cushioned, wheel penetration and hydraulically adjustable or retractable skis need special considerations beyond the AC.
notes.source: AC 43.13-2C, Acceptable Methods, Techniques, and Practices – Aircraft Alterations (29 July 2026), Chapter 6, Ski Installations, 6.1, p. 6-1
notes.evidence: The information provided for main ski and nose ski installations applies to wheel replacement skis only.

notes.front: In AC 43.13-2C, what is it for skis to “dump”, and what causes it?
notes.back: The skis rotate nose down in flight; improper rigging or weak springs or shock cords cause it.
notes.explanation: It can make the aeroplane uncontrollable or cause it to break up in flight.
notes.source: AC 43.13-2C, Acceptable Methods, Techniques, and Practices – Aircraft Alterations (29 July 2026), Chapter 6, Ski Installations, 6.2, p. 6-1
notes.evidence: Improper rigging, weak springs or shock cords, or all, can cause the skis to "dump," or rotate nose down in flight, possibly rendering the airplane uncontrollable or causing it to break up in flight.

notes.front: Under AC 43.13-2C chapter 6, only an aeroplane {{c1::approved for operation on skis}} is eligible for a ski installation.
notes.explanation: Eligibility can be checked in the aircraft specifications, the type certificate data sheet or the supplemental type certificates.
notes.source: AC 43.13-2C, Acceptable Methods, Techniques, and Practices – Aircraft Alterations (29 July 2026), Chapter 6, Ski Installations, 6.4.1, p. 6-1
notes.evidence: Only an airplane approved for operation on skis is eligible for ski installations in accordance with this chapter.

notes.front: Under AC 43.13-2C, how tall may a ski pedestal be?
notes.back: No more than 130 percent of the standard tyre’s static rolling radius, measured from the ski’s bottom to the axle centreline.
notes.explanation: The limit avoids excessive bending moments on the landing gear and its attachment structure.
notes.source: AC 43.13-2C, Acceptable Methods, Techniques, and Practices – Aircraft Alterations (29 July 2026), Chapter 6, Ski Installations, 6.4.5, p. 6-2
notes.evidence: In order to avoid excessive bending moments on the landing gear and attachment structure, the ski pedestal height measured from the bottom surface of the ski to the axle centerline must not exceed 130 percent of the static rolling radius of the standard tire approved for the airplane

notes.front: What does AC 43.13-2C call wheel and tyre combinations larger than originally certificated?
notes.back: Tundra tire modifications.
notes.explanation: They better adapt aeroplanes working from harsh or rough terrain to that flying environment.
notes.source: AC 43.13-2C, Acceptable Methods, Techniques, and Practices – Aircraft Alterations (29 July 2026), Chapter 14, Larger Tire Installations, 14.1, p. 14-1
notes.evidence: These larger wheel/tire combinations are commonly referred to as tundra tire modifications and better adapt airplanes to a particular operating flying environment.

notes.front: To which aeroplanes and tyre sizes does AC 43.13-2C’s larger tyre chapter generally apply?
notes.back: Fixed-gear aeroplanes under 6,000 pounds gross takeoff weight, with tyres and wheels no more than 130 percent of the standard combination.
notes.explanation: Both conditions apply together: a light fixed-gear aeroplane and a limited size increase.
notes.source: AC 43.13-2C, Acceptable Methods, Techniques, and Practices – Aircraft Alterations (29 July 2026), Chapter 14, Larger Tire Installations, 14.1, p. 14-1
notes.evidence: The information provided in this chapter can generally be applied to fixed gear airplanes less than 6,000 pounds gross takeoff weight when installing tires and wheel assemblies that do not exceed 130 percent of the standard tire and wheel combination

notes.front: AC 43.13-2C notes evidence of increased {{c1::structural failure of the landing gear}} on aircraft with larger tyres.
notes.explanation: This evidence is why the AC warns that larger tyres may expose occupants to additional risks.
notes.source: AC 43.13-2C, Acceptable Methods, Techniques, and Practices – Aircraft Alterations (29 July 2026), Chapter 14, Larger Tire Installations, 14.2.2, p. 14-1
notes.evidence: Operation of airplanes with larger tires may expose the occupants to additional risks because there is evidence of increased structural failure of the landing gear or components on aircraft operating with these modifications.
